content.title: About
content.content: Cornbread is a classic American quick bread made from cornmeal, wheat flour, eggs, milk, and a leavening agent. It has a dense yet crumbly texture, a golden crust, and a mildly sweet flavor. The home recipe (2573) uses simple, pantry‑ready ingredients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cornbread originated in the United States in the 19th century as a fast way to use ground corn.
In the Southern states it is traditionally served with fried meats, beans, and gravies.
The classic recipe relies on baking powder or soda, not yeast, to rise.
Cornmeal gives the bread its distinctive yellow hue.
Some regional versions add honey or maple syrup for extra sweetness.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Cornbread provides steady energy through slowly digestible carbs, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Cornmeal is rich in fiber, which supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The recipe supplies thiamine (B1), niacin (B3), and folate, essential for metabolic processes.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Corn provides carotenoids and phenolic compounds that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When prepared with minimal butter or oil, cornbread remains a relatively low‑fat option.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cornmeal.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Cornbread can raise blood glucose quickly, so people with diabetes should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Added salt or leavening agents increase sodium levels; portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve warm, sliced. Spread with butter, honey, or jam, use as a base for sandwiches, or pair with soups, stews, and fried dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cornbread in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 1 week) or freeze wrapped tightly in plastic.

content.title: About
content.content: Dessert sauce (5050) is a thick sweet sauce made from fruit purées, sugar and natural flavorings. It is intended for drizzling over cakes, ice cream, pancakes and other desserts, giving them a vivid fruit taste and a glossy finish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sauce is produced in small batches to preserve the freshness and aroma of the fruits.
Only natural ingredients are used, without artificial colors or preservatives.
5050 indicates the balance of sweetness and acidity (50 % sugar, 50 % fruit).
The sauce can serve as a base for creating custom fruit glazes and jams.
It keeps in the refrigerator for up to 6 months after opening if tightly sealed.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Fruit components provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike creamy sauces, the dessert sauce contains virtually no fat, making it a lighter option.

items.title: Source of natural sugars
items.content: The sugar comes from fruit, offering a slower rise in blood glucose compared with refined sugar.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Small amounts of fruit fiber help maintain normal bowel function.

items.title: Fruit allergy
items.content: People allergic to specific fruits (e.g., strawberry or mango) should check the ingredient list.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Despite being natural, the sauce contains a notable amount of sugar and should be limited for individuals with diabetes.

items.title: Storage after opening
items.content: Once opened, keep the sauce refrigerated and use within 2‑3 weeks to prevent microbial growth.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Drizzle the sauce over a finished cake, ice cream, pancakes or waffles. It can also be stirred into yogurt, cottage cheese, or used as a filling for layered desserts. For a thinner consistency, dilute with a small amount of water or juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened package in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep it refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C, tightly sealed. Discard the product if it develops a fermented smell or changes color.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg, whole, raw is a complete chicken egg that has not undergone any heat treatment. It contains both the yolk and the white, providing high-quality protein, vitamins, and minerals. Eggs are one of the most affordable and nutrient‑dense foods worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken eggs contain all essential amino acids needed by humans.
A typical large egg weighs about 50 g, with roughly 30 g of white and 20 g of yolk.
Unwashed eggs can be stored in the refrigerator for 3–4 weeks.
The shell is mainly calcium carbonate, a natural source of calcium for bones.
Raw eggs are commonly used in sauces, desserts, and batters.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: One egg provides about 6 g of complete protein that supports muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The yolk supplies vitamin B12, riboflavin (B2), and folate, important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Source of choline and lecithin
items.content: These compounds aid fat metabolism and support liver function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Eggs contain iron, zinc, selenium, and phosphorus, which are essential for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in the yolk protect the eyes from age‑related degeneration.

items.title: Salmonella risk
items.content: Raw eggs may be contaminated with Salmonella bacteria, so people with weakened immunity, pregnant women, and young children should avoid them.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Egg white proteins are common allergens, especially in children.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: A yolk contains about 186 mg of cholesterol; individuals with hypercholesterolemia should limit intake.

items.title: Shell contamination
items.content: The shell surface can harbor microbes; it should be rinsed before cracking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw eggs are used in sauces (e.g., hollandaise), desserts (custards, tiramisu), and baking to improve texture. Egg whites can be whipped into meringue, and yolks can be blended into smoothies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store eggs in the refrigerator at 1–4 °C in their original carton. Do not wash them before storage to preserve the natural protective coating. Discard any egg with an off‑odor or cracks.

content.title: About
content.content: Energy drink No Fear (5502) is a non‑alcoholic beverage containing caffeine, taurine, B‑vitamins and sugar (or its substitutes). It is designed to boost alertness, improve concentration and increase physical endurance. The drink has a distinctive fruity flavor and is sold in 250 ml and 500 ml cans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: No Fear was first launched in 2005 as part of an energy‑drink line aimed at the youth market.
A 250 ml can contains about 80 mg of caffeine, roughly the amount in a shot of espresso.
The formula includes vitamins B2, B3, B5, B6 and B12, which support metabolic processes.
No Fear is marketed as a "drink without limits" and its advertising often features extreme sports.
In some countries a sugar‑free version sweetened with stevia is available.

items.title: Increased energy
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, temporarily raising alertness and reducing feelings of fatigue.

items.title: Improved focus
items.content: Taurine and B‑vitamins help the brain work more efficiently, enhancing attention and reaction time.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Vitamins B5 and B6 are involved in converting food into usable energy, potentially speeding up metabolism.

items.title: Recovery after exertion
items.content: Sugar (or its substitutes) quickly replenishes glucose stores, while electrolytes aid in restoring fluid balance.

items.title: Antioxidant effect
items.content: Some variants are fortified with vitamin C, which protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Excessive caffeine intake
items.content: High caffeine doses can cause nervousness, insomnia, rapid heartbeat and increased blood pressure.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Regular consumption of high‑sugar drinks raises the risk of tooth decay, obesity and type‑2 diabetes.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to taurine, glucuronolactone or artificial flavorings.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Caffeine may amplify the effects of stimulants and certain drugs, so intake should be limited when taking medication.

items.title: Not for children or pregnant women
items.content: Due to its high caffeine and stimulant levels, the drink is not recommended for children, adolescents, pregnant or nursing women.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Consume No Fear chilled, straight from the can. For best results drink it about 30 minutes before physical activity or when energy drops. Do not mix with alcohol.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the drink in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep it refrigerated and consume within 24 hours.

turkey-light-meat-breaded-baked-or-fried.title: Turkey, light meat, breaded, baked or fried, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a bird from the pheasant family, primarily raised for its tender white meat. Breaded turkey meat can be baked in the oven or fried in a pan. The skin is usually removed before cooking because it contains more fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White turkey meat contains less fat than dark meat and is considered more diet‑friendly.
Breadings are often made from whole‑grain breadcrumbs, increasing the fiber content.
Baked breaded meat retains more nutrients than fried versions.
Turkey is a traditional holiday dish in many countries, especially the United States (Thanksgiving).
Turkey skin is rich in collagen but is usually omitted in low‑fat recipes due to its higher fat content.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: White turkey meat provides about 23 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: It contains less than 2 g of fat per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey is rich in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies phosphorus, selenium and zinc – essential for bones, immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The product does not cause a rapid rise in blood sugar, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bird meat.

items.title: Contamination during frying
items.content: High‑heat frying can produce acrylamide and other potentially harmful compounds.

items.title: Sodium in breading
items.content: Pre‑breaded products often contain added salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Proper cooking
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor pathogens such as Salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Breaded turkey can be baked at 180‑200 °C until golden brown or quickly pan‑fried with a small amount of oil. Serve with vegetable sides, whole‑grain grains or fresh salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked product in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Freeze in portion‑sized bags at –18 °C for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey or chicken sausage is a lean meat product made from ground turkey or chicken, seasoned with herbs and spices and sometimes blended with a small amount of fat for juiciness. It has a mild flavor, low saturated‑fat content, and a high protein level, making it a popular choice for health‑conscious eaters.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey and chicken contain fewer calories than beef or pork, so their sausages are often chosen for diet plans.
Traditional versions are made from ground meat, but modern varieties may include whole‑muscle pieces for texture.
In the US and Canada, turkey sausage gained popularity in the 1990s as an alternative to traditional pork sausage.
Common flavor enhancers include paprika, garlic, thyme, and other aromatic spices.
Some manufacturers add probiotics to support digestive health.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Turkey or chicken sausage provides about 15‑20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with conventional pork sausage, it contains significantly less saturated fat, which is better for heart health.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The product supplies niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, essential for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of selenium and zinc
items.content: These trace minerals help maintain immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low calorie count
items.content: Approximately 120‑150 kcal per 100 g, making it convenient for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey or chicken.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Like most sausages, it can be high in sodium; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can allow pathogens such as Salmonella to grow.

items.title: Additives and preservatives
items.content: Certain brands contain nitrites or artificial flavorings, which may be undesirable for sensitive consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sausage can be eaten cold as sliced deli meat, added to sandwiches, salads, or cooked dishes. It also reheats well on a skillet, in the microwave, or baked in the oven. For a lighter option, choose varieties without extra fat and with minimal salt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the sausage refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container for up to 5‑7 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C, where it retains quality for 2‑3 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration; discard if any signs of spoilage appear.
